newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Drought looms over Brazil 96/97 corn crop-growers.
newsitem.headline: Drought looms over Brazil 96/97 corn crop-growers.

text.p: Brazil is due to harvest a 1996/97 corn crop of 33 to 34 million tonnes, but it could be as low as 32 million tonnes if rains don't come soon to key producing state Rio Grande do Sul, growers said.
Harvesting was set to begin from January 15 in the east of Parana state and weather conditions there were optimal.
"The corn is in very good condition," said Flavio Turra, agronomist at the Parana cooperatives organisation Ocepar. "Productivity is also good and climate conditions have been favourable so far."
Independent consultants Safras e Mercado's most recent forecast was for a 1996/97 corn crop of 33.4 million tonnes, up from 30.4 million tonnes in 1995/96.

But in Rio Grande do Sul, which traditionally starts planting later, much of the crop was still in the critical flowering stage and drought was threatening to wipe out up to a third of the state's production.
"More than 20 percent of the crop is in the critical flowering and pod formation stage," said Ronaldo Matzenauer at the Rio Grande do Sul agricultural secretariat.
"If it doesn't rain in the next 10 to 15 days, we will lose at least 20 percent of the crop," he said.
The state was expected to produce five million tonnes of corn in 1996/97, but without rains this could drop to between 3.5 and four million tonnes, Matzenauer said.
If it rained within a week, farmers could still get a good yield from corn planted after mid-November.
"I think the total Brazilian crop should be between 32 and 33 million tonnes in 1996/97, but if the drought persists it could be 32 million," he said.

Fernando Martins, agronomist at the Cotrijal cooperative in Nao-Me-Toque, said 35 to 40 percent of the crop had been destroyed by drought although he added conditions varied widely thoughout the state.

He estimated that both planted area and production during the second harvest, or "safrinha", could fall by 50 percent in Rio Grande do Sul as the dry weather and low prices discouraged farmers from planting corn.

Farmers in Parana were similarly likely to be put off planting additional corn, but rather than dropping sharply planted area there should remain stable for the safrinha, according to Turra at Ocepar.
Because sowing started earlier in Parana, most of the state's crop entered the flowering phase in December, coinciding with good rains. The current dry conditions were ideal for harvesting.
Parana was forecast to produce 6.5 million tonnes in the first harvest and an additional 1.5 million tonnes in the safrinha, Turra said.

"It is very likely that this production level will be exceeded," he said. "The total Brazil crop is more likely to be around 34 million tonnes, due to the favorable climactic conditions we are seeing right now."

Nonetheless, exports were unlikely to jump sharply in 1996/97 even after the removal of a state export tax in September because internal demand was tight and domestic prices were broadly in line with international markets.

"We don't think we should be exporting two million tonnes," Turra said, referring to a previous forecast by a Sao Paulo bourse official. "We think it will be around 500,000 tonnes, a little more than was exported last harvest."
Brazil exported 300,000 to 400,000 tonnes in the May to July period last year.
"We could try to increase sales to new markets like Japan and China," Turra said. "But Japan is very demanding in terms of continuity of supply."
Instead, Brazil was likely to continue exporting to regular clients such as Morocco and Libya and could also supply occasional clients like South Africa with orders of around 50,000 tonnes.
